strengths: Soundness: The logical reductions in Theorems 5.1 and 6.1 are clear and convincing under the stated nonempty-minimizer assumption. Expressing optimality through quantified polynomial comparisons accommodates nonsmooth objectives and distinct training and validation losses without the earlier geometric regularity assumptions.

Significance: A framework for bounding the statistical complexity of implicitly defined, multidimensional hyperparameter losses is useful. The extension to optimistic bilevel validation objectives and semialgebraic regularizers meaningfully broadens the setting beyond scalar tuning.

Originality: The contribution lies primarily in combining quantitative quantifier elimination with instance-specific Goldberg–Jerrum analysis. The weighted group-lasso encoding illustrates how this perspective can handle objectives beyond piecewise polynomials.

Presentation and reproducibility: The progression from logical definitions to general bounds and applications is accessible, and the appendices supply substantial proof detail. The discussion appropriately identifies general lower bounds and extensions beyond semialgebraic objectives as open questions. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: Theorem 7.2's rational-composition degree bound is incorrect under Assumption 7.1 as written. Coordinatewise degree bounds do not imply that substituting a vector of rational functions multiplies degrees. For example, theta_i(alpha)=1/(alpha+a_i) has degree one in every coordinate, while the linear objective g_x(theta)=sum_i c_i(x)theta_i generally becomes a rational function of degree d. Appendix F.1 nevertheless asserts Delta_total=Delta_k Delta_path and eliminates dimension dependence. This is substantive: with distinct positive a_i, interpolation at d parameter values allows instance-specific coefficients to encode arbitrary sign patterns, giving pseudodimension growing at least logarithmically with d despite constant stated path and objective complexities. A common-denominator assumption or a corrected degree bound is needed.

Application assumptions: Section 8 does not explicitly restrict regularization weights to be nonnegative, although the convexity and duality argument in Appendix G.2 requires this. Full column rank alone does not supply that condition. For group lasso, negative weights can even make the inner problem unbounded when A has a null direction. The applications also assert bounded loss classes without specifying data restrictions or clipping that would ensure a uniform H. These conditions should be stated explicitly to support the advertised sample-complexity conclusions.

Originality and significance: The broad claims of the 'first general' multidimensional tuning guarantees need more careful qualification. The manuscript itself recovers an existing two-parameter ElasticNet result and identifies earlier first-order-logic bounds from Goldberg–Jerrum. The precise novelty is therefore the scope and quantitative improvement of the framework, rather than multidimensional tuning generally. A more detailed comparison of assumptions and resulting rates would make the significance easier to assess; the only demonstrated tightness example recovers an existing result.

Presentation and proof reproducibility: Several mathematical inconsistencies impede verification. Definition 2.1 uses a three-valued sign function and exactly 2^N realized patterns instead of the standard binary threshold shattering definition. Appendix C gives an incorrect graph for x/y and omits absolute values in its odd-p norm example. Appendix B replaces K by M in quantifier-block products, and Appendix G.1 uses b instead of b' in the validation predicate. In addition, Appendix G.2 counts active-set regions but does not explicitly bound the boundary predicates required by Theorem 7.2. These issues warrant a systematic proof revision.

Scope of guarantees: The framework establishes statistical guarantees conditional on solving the outer empirical optimization problem; it supplies neither a tuning algorithm nor computational guarantees. Moreover, optimistic selection among training minimizers need not match the output of an actual training procedure. The optimistic convention is disclosed, but its operational implications and the distinction between statistical learnability and practical tuning should be developed more clearly.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful theoretical problem: learning multiple hyperparameters across problem instances when validation performance depends implicitly on an inner optimization. Handling distinct training and validation objectives and nonunique training minimizers substantially broadens the setting.

Soundness: The threshold encodings in Theorems 5.1 and 6.1 are convincing under the standing assumptions. In particular, expressing optimistic validation loss through a universal optimality condition provides a clean route to quantifier elimination without requiring smooth solution paths.

Originality: The combination of quantitative quantifier elimination with the refined Goldberg–Jerrum framework offers a useful synthesis. Extending the analysis beyond piecewise polynomials through auxiliary variables for group norms is also worthwhile.

Presentation and reproducibility: The main argument is organized coherently, and the appendices provide substantial proof details. Recovering the known ElasticNet rate supplies a useful consistency check. The paper appropriately acknowledges that general matching lower bounds remain open; no material research-ethics concerns are evident.
weaknesses: Soundness—Theorem 7.2 has a substantive degree-counting problem. Appendix F.1 asserts that substituting a vector of rational functions into the validation objective gives degree Δk·Δpath. Different coordinates can have different denominators, so this is generally false. For example, θj(α)=1/(α+j) has coordinatewise degree one, but the linear objective Σj ajθj(α) can have denominator degree d. These paths can arise as unique minimizers of Σj((α+j)θj−1)^2 on a bounded box. Varying the coefficients aj permits interpolation of arbitrary signs at d hyperparameter values, yielding pseudo-dimension growing at least as log d, whereas the stated structural parameters imply a constant bound. A common-denominator assumption or a revised dimension-dependent bound is needed.

Soundness—The application domains omit essential restrictions on regularization weights. Sections 8.1–8.2 specify real-valued α without requiring nonnegative coordinates. Negative weights can make the group-lasso objective unbounded below. For fused lasso, full column rank does not restore convexity when weights are negative, and the asserted dual constraints |ui|≤αi become infeasible. Thus the application theorems require explicit parameter-domain assumptions.

Proof completeness: Appendix G.2 bounds the number of active-set regions by 3^p and treats this as Mpath, although Assumption 7.1 defines Mpath as the number of boundary functions and separately requires Tpath. Each region can require multiple inequalities. The claimed O(d²) rate appears plausibly repairable, but the necessary boundary and piece counts are not actually established. Appendix G.1 also uses b instead of b′ in the validation predicate.

Significance and originality: The broad claims of the first general guarantees for multidimensional tuning need tighter qualification. The paper itself discusses earlier multidimensional ElasticNet guarantees and an existing first-order-logic VC-dimension framework. Its contribution is more specifically a quantitative extension for implicitly defined bilevel losses. The comparison with Goldberg–Jerrum should explain which improvements follow from fixing each instance before applying the existing refined framework.

Presentation and limitations: Several mathematical inaccuracies impede verification: Definition 2.1 uses ternary sign-pattern cardinality rather than the standard binary shattering condition; Appendix C omits absolute values in its formula for general integer-p norms and incorrectly describes the graph of division. Beyond correcting these, the paper should distinguish statistical learnability from computationally feasible tuning and explain exact ERM attainment under its discontinuous objectives. These issues, together with the unresolved refined theorem, prevent reliable reuse despite the merits of the general framework.

strengths: Soundness: The logical encoding of training optimality and optimistic validation loss in Sections 5–6 is convincing. In particular, the universal–existential formulation accommodates multiple training minimizers without requiring smoothness or regular solution paths.

Significance: Explicit sample-complexity guarantees for multidimensional, implicitly defined hyperparameter losses are useful. The weighted group-lasso application illustrates how auxiliary variables extend the framework beyond piecewise polynomial objectives.

Originality: Combining quantitative quantifier elimination with the refined Goldberg–Jerrum framework provides a useful unifying perspective. The distinction between training and validation objectives meaningfully extends the setting emphasized in the manuscript.

Presentation and reproducibility: The paper has a clear progression from the general framework to specialized applications, and supplies substantial proofs in the appendices. Recovering the known ElasticNet rate provides a helpful consistency check. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—Theorem 7.2 has a substantive gap: Appendix F.1 claims that substituting a vector of rational functions into a degree-Δk objective produces degree at most Δk·Δpath. This fails when coordinates have different denominators. For example, θ_i(α)=1/(α+c_i), with distinct positive c_i, has coordinatewise degree one, but g_x(θ)=(Σ_i x_iθ_i)^2 generally produces rational degree proportional to d. Thus the asserted removal of dependence on model dimension is unsupported without a common-denominator assumption or a revised degree bound.

This issue can invalidate the bound itself, rather than merely its proof. The preceding path is the unique minimizer of Σ_i((α+c_i)θ_i−1)^2 on a suitable compact box. With d=2^N distinct α values, the associated Cauchy matrix is invertible, so coefficients for N validation objectives can interpolate every binary labeling across those α values. Squaring and thresholding at 1/2 therefore shatters N instances, while Theorem 7.2 predicts O(1) because p=1, both functions have one piece, and the stated degree parameters are constant. The theorem needs correction before others can reliably use it.

Assumptions and reproducibility: Sections 8.1–8.2 do not explicitly restrict regularization weights to be nonnegative. Negative weights can destroy the convexity used in Appendix G.2 and can make the group-lasso objective unbounded below. Also, bounded losses are stipulated without specifying corresponding restrictions on the regression instance distribution. These conditions should be made explicit in the application statements.

Limitations: The optimistic validation loss selects the best validation performance among all training minimizers; an ordinary training solver need not implement this selection. Although the convention is acknowledged, its practical implications deserve discussion. Likewise, compact hyperparameter domains and piecewise polynomial objectives do not ensure that the exact outer ERM assumed in Theorem 2.2 exists; an approximate-ERM formulation would address this gap.

Presentation and significance: The opening claim that existing guarantees concern only scalar hyperparameters is too broad given the multidimensional ElasticNet result discussed in Appendix F.2. The novelty should be scoped to the general implicit-optimization framework. Definition 2.1 also uses three-valued signs and a cardinality-equals-2^N condition instead of the standard binary shattering definition. The acknowledged absence of general lower bounds is reasonable, but leaves the sharpness of the main general rates unresolved. Overall, the promising framework does not compensate for the incorrect refined theorem.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful statistical question: learning multiple hyperparameters across problem instances when performance is defined through an inner optimization problem. Separating training and validation objectives substantially broadens the setting.

Soundness: The central reductions in Theorems 5.1 and 6.1 are convincing. Encoding optimal-value thresholds with universal quantification, and validation-loss thresholds with a universal–existential formula, provides a clean route from quantifier elimination to pseudo-dimension bounds without boundary regularity assumptions.

Originality: Although the framework combines established quantifier-elimination and Goldberg–Jerrum tools, specializing formulas to fixed instances and thresholds yields a useful refinement. The polynomial lower-bound construction in Appendix D.2 adds substantive technical content through its stabilization of discrete bit extraction under continuous optimization.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript explains the logical reductions accessibly and supplies extensive proofs and application derivations. This is a theoretical contribution, so the absence of experiments is not itself a weakness. The discussion appropriately identifies unresolved lower bounds and extensions beyond semialgebraic objectives.
weaknesses: Soundness—Theorem 7.2 is not established under the stated assumptions. Appendix F.1 asserts that substituting a vector of rational functions into a degree-Delta_k objective produces degree at most Delta_k times Delta_path. Coordinate-specific denominators invalidate this claim. For example, theta_i(alpha)=1/(alpha+c_i) has coordinate degree one, but a linear objective sum_i a_i theta_i generally has denominator degree d. More strongly, varying the linear coefficients permits interpolation at d distinct hyperparameter values and can produce pseudo-dimension growing as log d, whereas the stated constant-complexity, single-piece bound is independent of d. The result needs an additional common-denominator assumption or a corrected dimension-dependent bound. This directly undermines the advertised general refinement in Section 7, although the particular applications may retain their rates after repair.

Soundness—The weighted group-lasso proof contains an incorrect validation predicate. Appendix G.1 defines T2 using ||A' theta-b||^2, whereas Equation (4) specifies ||A' theta-b'||^2. The displayed formula therefore describes a different loss and can be dimensionally undefined when training and validation sample counts differ. This appears repairable, but the application theorem is not proved by the formula as written.

Assumptions and reproducibility: Section 8 does not explicitly restrict regularization weights to be nonnegative. The fused-lasso proof relies on convexity and the dual constraints |u_i| <= alpha_i; these arguments do not apply to negative weights. Negative group-lasso weights can also destroy existence of a minimizer for rank-deficient designs. The application statements should specify the hyperparameter domain and conditions ensuring nonempty solution sets and uniformly bounded validation losses.

Significance and scope: The guarantees concern an optimistic bilevel loss that selects the best validation performance among training minimizers. Proposition 6.2 retains this selection over approximate minimizers; it does not establish a guarantee for an arbitrary approximate solver's output. The manuscript should distinguish this statistical target from ordinary solver-based tuning and clarify that sample complexity does not provide an efficient ERM algorithm.

Presentation and precision: Several foundational statements require correction. Definition 2.1 counts ternary sign patterns and requires exactly 2^N patterns, rather than requiring all binary threshold labelings. Proposition 6.2 references Theorem 5.1's assumptions, which do not impose the needed structure on g. Appendix C's norm graph omits absolute values for odd powers, and its claimed graph of x/y is incorrect. Together with the substantive rational-composition issue, these errors reduce confidence in the manuscript's mathematical reliability.

Overall assessment: The core framework has clear merit, and no material research-ethics concern is apparent. However, a general theorem is false under its stated assumptions, and application proofs and domains need correction. These technical issues prevent acceptance in the current form.

strengths: Soundness: The core reduction in Theorems 4.1, 5.1, and 6.1 is coherent: encode loss thresholds in polynomial first-order logic, eliminate quantifiers, and apply a Goldberg–Jerrum bound. The validation-loss formulation correctly accommodates multiple training minimizers through optimistic bilevel optimization.

Significance: Extending the implicit-optimization setting to multiple hyperparameters and distinct training and validation objectives is useful. Avoiding the earlier geometric regularity assumptions broadens the framework's applicability.

Originality: The lower-bound construction in Theorem 5.2 combines bit extraction with a substantive stabilization argument that transfers discrete grid behavior to continuous minimization. This is a meaningful contribution beyond applying existing quantifier-elimination results.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript provides extensive proofs and explicit complexity parameters, making much of the argument independently checkable. The discussion acknowledges unresolved general bilevel lower bounds and the restriction to semialgebraic objectives. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—Theorem 7.2 has a substantive degree-counting error. Appendix F.1 asserts that substituting a vector of rational functions into a degree-Delta_k objective yields degree at most Delta_k times Delta_path. With different coordinate denominators, this is false: theta_i(alpha)=1/(alpha+c_i) has coordinate degree one, but a linear objective sum_i a_i theta_i generally has denominator degree d. Assumption 7.1 does not require a common denominator of bounded degree. This undermines the claimed dimension-independent bound; rational interpolation with these coordinates can encode increasingly many threshold patterns as d grows. The theorem needs stronger assumptions or a corrected degree bound.

Soundness—The application domains omit necessary restrictions on regularization weights. Section 8 allows alpha in R^p. For weighted group lasso, negative weights can make the objective unbounded below, for example with A=0, contradicting the required nonempty minimizer set. For weighted fused lasso, the convexity argument and dual constraints |u_i|<=alpha_i in Appendix G.2 require nonnegative weights; full column rank alone does not justify this derivation for negative weights. These conditions must be explicit in the application theorems.

Reproducibility—Appendix G.2 counts active-set regions and labels this quantity M_path, although Assumption 7.1 defines M_path as the number of boundary rational functions and separately requires T_path. The proof needs to bound both quantities and explain how the active-set representation satisfies that assumption. The O(d^2) conclusion may be repairable, but the supplied accounting does not establish it as written.

Significance and positioning: The abstract's assertion that existing guarantees concern scalar hyperparameters is too broad: Appendix F.2 itself discusses an existing two-parameter ElasticNet guarantee. The contribution should consistently be framed as extending a general implicit-optimization framework. Likewise, the lower bound leaves a factor-p gap in the degree-dependent term and does not match the full structural dependence of the upper bound.

Limitations: Proposition 6.2 analyzes the best validation loss over all approximately optimal training solutions, rather than the output of an arbitrary approximate training solver. The practical interpretation needs this distinction. Exact outer ERM attainment is also not ensured by compact parameter domains when discontinuous piecewise objectives are permitted; an approximate-ERM formulation would avoid this gap.

Presentation: Several formal inaccuracies impede verification. Definition 2.1 uses ternary signs and a cardinality condition instead of requiring all binary threshold labelings; Proposition 6.2 references Theorem 5.1 despite needing assumptions on g; and Appendix C gives incorrect graph formulas for odd-p norms and division. These are individually repairable, but collectively warrant a careful mathematical revision. The unresolved theorem and application issues outweigh the otherwise useful core contribution.

strengths: Soundness: The central approach in Theorems 4.1, 5.1, and 6.1 is coherent: encode loss-threshold events in polynomial first-order logic, apply quantitative quantifier elimination, and bound pseudo-dimension through the Goldberg–Jerrum framework. The validation-loss encoding accommodates nonunique training minimizers without requiring smooth solution paths.

Significance: Extending the implicit-optimization framework to multiple hyperparameters and distinct training and validation objectives is useful. Removing the earlier boundary regularity requirements substantially broadens applicability.

Originality: The lower-bound construction in Theorem 5.2 provides additional theoretical substance. Combining bit extraction with a coercive polynomial penalty and a uniform stabilization argument addresses the difficulty introduced by continuous inner optimization.

Presentation and reproducibility: The progression from the general framework to training loss, validation loss, and applications is understandable, and substantial proofs are supplied in the appendices. A theoretical evaluation is appropriate here; experiments are not necessary to establish the principal results. The conclusion appropriately acknowledges unresolved lower bounds and restrictions to semialgebraic objectives.
weaknesses: Soundness: Theorem 7.2 relies on an unjustified rational-composition degree bound. Appendix F.1 asserts that substitution gives degree Δk·Δpath, but different coordinates of the solution can have different denominators. For example, θi(α)=1/(α+ci) has coordinate degree one, whereas the linear objective Σi aiθi generally has denominator degree d. Such a path can arise as the unique minimizer of Σi((α+ci)θi−1)^2 on a compact interval. Varying the coefficients across instances permits increasingly complex threshold behavior despite fixed stated path and objective complexities. The theorem needs an explicit common-denominator assumption or a revised degree bound; its claimed removal of dependence on d is not established as written.

Application assumptions require correction. Section 8 allows α in Rp without explicitly requiring nonnegative regularization weights. In weighted group lasso, negative weights can make the training objective unbounded below, for example when A=0, violating the assumed existence of minimizers. The fused-lasso convex duality argument likewise requires nonnegative weights. These restrictions should be stated in the application theorems.

Significance and limitations: The guarantees concern optimistic selection of the best validation objective among all training minimizers. Proposition 6.2 retains this optimistic selection over all approximately optimal models; it does not establish guarantees for the particular model returned by an arbitrary approximate training algorithm. This distinction, and the lack of computational guarantees for outer ERM, should be explained more clearly when connecting the results to practical tuning.

Originality and positioning: The abstract's broad claim that existing guarantees concern only scalar hyperparameters is inconsistent with the cited ElasticNet results and the existing polynomial-FOL bound discussed in Section 4. The novelty should be framed around the particular implicit-optimization setting and quantitative improvements. Likewise, the lower bound leaves a factor-p gap in the degree-dependent term and uses unrestricted domains, so tightness claims need qualification.

Presentation and proof reproducibility: Several mathematical errors complicate verification: Definition 2.1 uses three-valued signs with an exact 2^N cardinality criterion rather than standard binary threshold shattering; Appendix B repeatedly substitutes M for K in quantifier-block products; and Appendix C gives incorrect graph formulas for odd-p norms and division. Appendix G.1 also uses b instead of b′ in its validation predicate. These are mostly repairable, but together with the substantive issue in Theorem 7.2 they warrant revision before acceptance.
